source_text: Haec patientiae ratio, haec disciplina, haec opera, — caelestis et uerae. scilicet Christiana non, ut illa patientia gentium terrae, falsa probrosa. nam ut in isto quoque domino diabolus aemularetur, quasi plane ex pari — nisi quod ipsa diuersitas mali et boni aequaliter magnitudinis par est — docuit et suos patientiam propriam, illam dico, quae maritos dote uenales aut lenociniis negotiantes uxorum potestatibus subicit, quae aucupandis orbitatibus omnem coacti obsequii laborem mentitis adfectionibus tolerat, quae uentris operarios contumeliosis patrociniis gulae subiectione libertatis addicit. talia nationes patientiae studia nouerunt et tanti boni nomen foedis operationibus occupant; patientes riualium et diuitum et inuitatorum, impatientes solius dei uiuunt. sed uiderint sua et sui praesidis, quam patientiam sub terra ignis expectat. ceterum nos amemus patientiam dei, patientiam Christi: rependamus illi quam pro nobis ipse dependit; offeramus patientiam spiritus, patientiam carnis, qui in resurrectionem carnis et spiritus credimus. -
thought_title: True Christian patience versus the devil's counterfeit
orientation: Tertullian is closing the treatise by contrasting the heavenly, true patience of Christians with the false, self-serving patience the devil has taught to pagans.
pass_a_gloss: This is the method of patience, this is the discipline, this is the work — of heavenly and true patience. Of course it is not Christian, as that patience of the pagans of the earth is false and shameful. For in this matter also the devil emulated the Lord, as if plainly from an equal position — except that the very difference of evil and good is equal in greatness — he taught also his own people a patience of his own, I mean that patience which subjects husbands who are for sale by dowry or who trade in pandering to the powers of wives, which endures every labor of forced obedience in feigned affections for the sake of hunting after childless estates, which hands over workers of the belly to insulting patronage by the subjection of freedom to gluttony. Such pursuits of patience have the pagans known, and they occupy the name of so great a good with foul activities; patient of rivals and of rich men and of inviters, impatient of God alone they live. But let them see to their own affairs and to their own protector, what patience the fire under the earth awaits. For the rest, let us love the patience of God, the patience of Christ: let us repay to him what he himself has paid out for us; let us offer the patience of the spirit, the patience of the flesh, we who believe in the resurrection of flesh and spirit.

choices.english: patience of the pagans of the earth
choices.why: Keeps the literal genitive chain and the contrast between earthly pagans and heavenly Christians; 'pagans' is the required glossary rendering for nationes/gens.
rejected: patience of the nations of the earth

choices.english: husbands who are for sale by dowry
choices.why: Literal rendering of the predicative adjective uenales with the instrumental dote, preserving the commercial metaphor of selling oneself for a wife's dowry.

choices.english: for the sake of hunting after childless estates
choices.why: Aucupor means to hunt or catch, and orbitas refers to childlessness or the estate of the childless; the gerundive with dative of purpose is rendered literally.
Literal rendering of the genitive of sphere, echoing Paul's 'whose god is the belly' language and keeping the bodily metaphor.

choices.term: rependamus illi quam pro nobis ipse dependit
choices.english: let us repay to him what he himself has paid out for us
choices.why: Preserves the financial metaphor of rependere/dependere (weighing out payment) and the reciprocal structure: our repayment answers his expenditure.
rejected: let us pay him back what he paid for us
let us return to him what he spent for us

choices.english: the patience of the spirit, the patience of the flesh
choices.why: Keeps the parallel genitive constructions and the required glossary terms 'spirit' and 'flesh'.
rejected: patience in spirit and in flesh

pass_b_english: This is the principle of patience, this its discipline, this its work—heavenly and true. It is not, of course, the pagan patience of the peoples of the earth, which is false and shameful. For in this matter too the devil wanted to rival the Lord, as if on equal terms—except that the very difference between evil and good is matched by an equal greatness. He taught his own followers a patience of his own: the patience, I mean, that subjects husbands who are for sale by dowry, or who trade on their wives' prostitution, to the power of their wives; that endures every labor of forced obedience with feigned affection for the sake of hunting after childless estates; that binds workers of the belly to insulting patronage by surrendering their freedom to gluttony. Such are the pursuits of patience that the pagans know, and they occupy the name of so great a good with filthy practices. Patient toward rivals, toward the rich, toward those who are invited, they live impatient toward God alone. But let them look to their own affairs and their own patron, and to what patience the fire under the earth awaits. As for us, let us love the patience of God and the patience of Christ. Let us repay to him what he himself has paid out for us. Let us offer the patience of the spirit and the patience of the flesh, we who believe in the resurrection of flesh and spirit.

problems.why: Latin refers to the invited (those who are invited), not the inviters.
problems.ruling: inuitatorum = 'of the invited,' passive participle, not 'those who invite.' English reverses agency, misleading the reader.

fixed: Changed 'those who invite them' to 'those who are invited' because 'inuitatorum' is genitive plural of 'invitati' (the invited), not the inviters.

problems.quote: It is not, of course, the Christian version of that patience of the pagans of the earth, which is false and shameful.
problems.source_quote: scilicet Christiana non, ut illa patientia gentium terrae, falsa probrosa.
problems.why: Latin says the described patience is not Christian but the pagan kind; English reverses the relationship.
problems.fix: It is not, of course, the pagan patience of the peoples of the earth, which is false and shameful.
problems.ruling: Latin 'Christiana non, ut illa patientia gentium' means not Christian but like pagan patience; English 'Christian version of that patience' reverses negation.

edits.old: It is not, of course, the Christian version of that patience of the pagans of the earth, which is false and shameful.
edits.new: It is not, of course, the pagan patience of the peoples of the earth, which is false and shameful.

fixed: Negation: source 'scilicet Christiana non, ut illa patientia gentium terrae, falsa probrosa' means the patience described is not Christian but the pagan kind; English reversed the relationship. Fixed to 'It is not, of course, the pagan patience of the peoples of the earth, which is false and shameful.'

last_rejected.quote: they live impatient toward God alone.
last_rejected.why: Latin says the impatient live for the one God, not that they are impatient toward God; agency and meaning reversed.
last_rejected.fix: the impatient live for the one God alone.
last_rejected.ruling: impatientes solius dei uiuunt: 'impatientes' governs 'solius dei'—they live impatient toward God alone. Standard Latin grammar supports the English.
